title: Amos 9:1–10
context: Amos sees the Lord standing beside the altar and commanding a blow that brings the sanctuary down. No one will escape, whether in Sheol, heaven, Carmel, or the sea, and even in captivity the sword will find them. A hymn names the LORD as the one who touches the land and builds his rooms in the heavens. The LORD then asks whether Israel is not like the Ethiopians to him, since he also brought the Philistines from Caphtor and the Syrians from Kir. He will destroy the sinful kingdom, yet not utterly destroy the house of Jacob; he will sift Israel as in a sieve, and the sinners who say evil will not overtake them will die. Shared ground: both traditions hear here that covenant privilege brings no immunity from judgment and that the LORD preserves a remnant. The Deuteronomy 7:7 box treats Israel’s election, and the Isaiah 10:22 and Romans 11:5 boxes treat the remnant.

verses.text: I saw the Lord standing beside the altar, and he said, “Strike the tops of the pillars, that the thresholds may shake. Break them in pieces on the head of all of them. I will kill the last of them with the sword. Not one of them will flee away. Not one of them will escape.
verses.arminianNotes: I saw the Lord standing beside the altar, Arminian readers see the final vision beginning at the altar, the place of worship, where the LORD commands the structure to be struck.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the altar is not named, and many think of Bethel (compare 3:14), though this is uncertain. Not one of them will escape the coming judgment.

verses.text: Though they dig into Sheol, there my hand will take them; and though they climb up to heaven, there I will bring them down.
verses.arminianNotes: Though they dig into Sheol, there my hand will take them; Arminian readers see that there is no hiding from the LORD, whether in the depths or in the heights.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers compare Psalm 139:7-10, where the LORD’s presence reaches heaven and Sheol, though there it brings comfort and here it brings judgment. The texts are named side by side.

verses.text: Though they hide themselves in the top of Carmel, I will search and take them out from there; and though they be hidden from my sight in the bottom of the sea, there I will command the serpent, and it will bite them.
verses.arminianNotes: Though they hide themselves in the top of Carmel, Arminian readers see the search reaching mountain and sea alike, so that the LORD’s judgment cannot be escaped.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the serpent in the sea is commanded by the LORD, who rules every creature. Carmel is the headland on Israel’s coast, a well-known place.

verses.text: Though they go into captivity before their enemies, there I will command the sword, and it will kill them. I will set my eyes on them for evil, and not for good.
verses.arminianNotes: Though they go into captivity before their enemies, Arminian readers see that even exile offers no refuge from judgment, for the sword will find them there.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the solemn phrase I will set my eyes on them for evil, and not for good. The Judges 9:23 box treats the LORD using enemies in judgment.

verses.text: For the Lord, the GOD of Armies, is he who touches the land and it melts, and all who dwell in it will mourn; and it will rise up wholly like the River, and will sink again, like the River of Egypt.
verses.arminianNotes: For the Lord, the GOD of Armies, is he who touches the land and it melts, Arminian readers see a hymn of praise to the LORD’s power over creation, inserted amid the judgment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the land rising and sinking like the River repeats 8:8. The hymn grounds the threats in the LORD’s sovereign rule over the earth.

verses.text: It is he who builds his rooms in the heavens, and has founded his vault on the earth; he who calls for the waters of the sea, and pours them out on the surface of the earth—the LORD is his name.
verses.arminianNotes: It is he who builds his rooms in the heavens, Arminian readers see the Creator who calls for the waters of the sea and pours them out on the earth, the LORD is his name.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that similar hymns appear in 4:13 and 5:8. The doxology reminds hearers that the one who judges is the Maker of heaven and earth.

verses.text: Are you not like the children of the Ethiopians to me, children of Israel?” says the LORD. “Haven’t I brought up Israel out of the land of Egypt, and the Philistines from Caphtor, and the Syrians from Kir?
verses.arminianNotes: Are you not like the children of the Ethiopians to me, children of Israel? Arminian readers see Israel’s election as a calling to covenant privilege and service that brings no immunity from judgment; see the Deuteronomy 7:7 box.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree that election is not a shield for sin, while seeing its ground in God’s unmerited love (Deuteronomy 7:7–8). The LORD also guided the Philistines from Caphtor and the Syrians from Kir, places whose locations are identified only tentatively.

verses.text: Behold, the eyes of the Lord GOD are on the sinful kingdom, and I will destroy it from off the surface of the earth, except that I will not utterly destroy the house of Jacob,” says the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: Behold, the eyes of the Lord GOD are on the sinful kingdom, Arminian readers see judgment on the sinful kingdom combined with mercy: I will not utterly destroy the house of Jacob.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the remnant preserved by God’s faithfulness; the Isaiah 10:22 box treats the remnant of Jacob. Shared ground: judgment and mercy stand together.

verses.text: “For behold, I will command, and I will sift the house of Israel among all the nations as grain is sifted in a sieve, yet not the least kernel will fall on the earth.
verses.arminianNotes: For behold, I will command, and I will sift the house of Israel among all the nations as grain is sifted in a sieve, Arminian readers see a sifting that separates the faithful from the unfaithful.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that not the least kernel will fall on the earth and see God’s preservation of his own; the Romans 11:5 box treats the remnant chosen by grace.

verses.text: All the sinners of my people will die by the sword, who say, ‘Evil won’t overtake nor meet us.’
verses.arminianNotes: All the sinners of my people will die by the sword, Arminian readers see judgment falling on those who presume on God’s favor, saying that evil will not overtake them.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the false security of those who say, Evil won’t overtake nor meet us. Both traditions read the verse as a warning against presumption.
